name: Amazonas
summary_text: Amazonas stands under Peru's national framework: the department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern, and none of the sources covering this territory contain Amazonas-specific content. What a trans visitor faces in Amazonas is the national statute book, national policing and national monitoring data.  Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities. On 20 February 2025 the Comision de Mujer y Familia of the Congress approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex. The exceptions are narrow: custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities. Venues would also be obliged not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The text still required plenary backing at that date, and the reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argued that the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.  On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis of 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.  The restriction reaches private as well as public life. INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so the document a visitor carries will generally carry the sex marker assigned at birth. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.  Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.  One case illustrates the pattern of violence and the delay of remedy. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots; Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, had been shot days earlier. Two killers were arrested in March 2023. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.  Hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.  The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.  Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.  Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.  One case illustrates the pattern of violence and the delay of remedy. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots; Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, had been shot days earlier. Two killers were arrested in March 2023. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.  Hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.  The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.  Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.  Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

name: CAR
summary_text: The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81.  No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, which allies planned to endorse to the 20th Congress on 28 July. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.  No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years, since 2000, without passage. The protections that do exist form a patchwork: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces, including Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, and in 32 cities and municipalities, alongside sectoral statutes. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment; the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.  Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; she called the attack traumatic, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIE Equality Bill.  Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex pairings are used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. There is no gender-matched placement. Official practice instead takes the form of administrative segregation: the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.  Local ordinances restrict presentation in public. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps.  Social visibility is high. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events and nightlife and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist; in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.  The Cordillera Administrative Region, created on 15 July 1987 and comprising Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Kalinga and Mountain Province centred on Baguio, is the country's only landlocked region and its least populated according to the 2020 Census of Population and Housing, with fewer residents than the national capital. It is home to numerous ethnic groups, including a majority-Igorot province, and a continuing Cordillera autonomy movement; the Cordillera People's Liberation Army ceasefire was secured by the Aquino government. Within this region, Kalinga province was formed out of Kalinga-Apayao on 8 May 1995 by Republic Act No. 7878 with Tabuk as capital.  In Kalinga, the inter-tribal customary justice system runs alongside the formal court system. Bodong and pagta holders resolve criminal and tribal offences, with Philippine National Police personnel, prosecutors and barangay officials participating in customary-law conflict resolution. This indigenous governance context developed against a history of resistance: Kalinga was a flashpoint between the Marcos martial-law government (declared September 1972) and its indigenous peoples over the Chico River Dam Project, which would have displaced about 100,000 indigenous people; the 24 April 1980 murder of tribal leader Macli-ing Dulag turned public opinion and made the dam dispute a landmark ancestral-domain case, and the September 1986 Mount Data Peace Accord created the Cordillera Autonomous Region, with later plebiscites failing to ratify autonomy.

sources.documents: Penal code criminalization of 'public expression of love' between persons of same sex, penalties including 6 months to 2 years imprisonment or 150,000-600,000 CFA francs fine, enhanced penalty when child involved, and that there were no reports police arrested or detained persons under these provisions in 2012; also societal discrimination against LGBT persons entrenched and attributed to Western influence.
